summary:
We developed Pixel Space Academy: The Lantern Mission, a free browser game in which students design and fly a crewed mission to the Moon, solo or as a four-player Mission Control team on their own devices.

Players begin with clear objectives and a science goal, then design Lantern-2 (their rocket) one decision at a time: orbit, power, structure, supplies, instruments and antenna. Live meters track mass, power, budget, data, communications and build time, and the design matures from concept to point design using NASA’s Concept Maturity Levels. Every choice changes the five missions as follows: a heavy spacecraft makes launch harder, solar power without a battery stalls in Earth’s shadow, and a small antenna leaves science data behind. A final report explains why the mission succeeded or failed, rates its risk, and compares the design with real NASA missions to encourage interest in young explorers. In multiplayer, each role sees different information, so teams must negotiate and communicate.


This matters because mission trade-offs are usually taught as abstract numbers. Our game lets students feel them, fail safely, understand why and try again. These features have been carefully incorporated into a fictional storyline that ends with a moral dilemma. Middle-school play testers loved it, showing that real mission-design thinking can be fun.
details:
What it does and how it works

Pixel Space Academy: The Lantern Mission is a free browser-based game where students design and fly their own crewed mission to the Moon. They can play alone or work together as a four-person Mission Control team. The goal is to complete the mission left unfinished by their mentor, Commander Lena Hart, who flew Lantern-1 to Shackleton Crater but turned back without explaining why.

Players begin with six mission objectives before moving on to designing Lantern-2. They make decisions about its science focus, orbit, power, structure, supplies and instruments. Live meters help them keep track of the budget, mass, power, build time, data and risk. Once the design is complete, they take on five missions, starting with launch and ending with collecting Moon samples. Each mission is affected by the decisions they made while building their spacecraft. At the end, they receive a report explaining their results. The story then leads to a final choice: should they share the Moon's ice with the world or keep it a secret?

In multiplayer mode, two to four players can join using a code, with each player using their own device. Everyone has a different role and access to different information, so communication and teamwork are necessary to complete the mission.

We used a pixelized design to keep the game UI/UX simple, drawing focus on the mission and the learning material while still incorporating fun and bold colors. Moreover, we saw that retro gaming styles were resurging, forming a multi-billion dollar global market.

Benefits

The game helps students understand engineering trade-offs by letting them experience them firsthand. Every decision affects the missions, and when something goes wrong, the game explains why using real numbers and a helpful tip. This allows students to learn from their mistakes and try again. Playing together also encourages teamwork and communication. Since the game is free, works in any browser and doesn't require accounts, it can easily be used in classrooms.

Intended impact

Our aim is to help students of all ages understand that successful space missions depend on careful decision-making, engineering trade-offs and teamwork. We also want them to see that these are skills they could develop and use themselves.

Teachers can use a single short session to introduce students to engineering design, orbits and the Moon. The final decision in the storyline also creates an opportunity to discuss who should own and have access to space resources. During our playtesting, middle-school students really enjoyed the game.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

The game is built as a single web page using HTML, CSS and JavaScript. We use the Canvas 2D API for the pixel-style graphics and the Web Audio API for sound. Multiplayer functionality is handled through Firebase Realtime Database, and the game is hosted on Netlify.

Google Colab was used for early prototypes, while Node.js test players helped us balance the game's difficulty. We also used Claude, an AI assistant, to help write and test code, with all development decisions and directions coming from our team. The game only requires an ordinary laptop, tablet or phone to run.

How it is creative

During our interviews, we found that a good story is what makes players connect with a game, so we took inspiration from games they already enjoy.

For example, we took inspiration from Resident Evil, where limited oxygen, food and fuel create tension. From Elden Ring, we borrowed the idea of revealing mysteries through the world itself rather than explaining everything directly. Red Dead Redemption inspired the mentor-centered storyline and the moral choice at the end, while Among the Sleep influenced how the final mission explores the darkness through the eyes of a young hero.

What makes our game different from most design tools is that players don't just design a spacecraft; they actually get to fly it. This makes the consequences of their decisions much more real. Each science focus rewards a different spacecraft design, multiplayer mode divides information between different roles, and real Apollo sample-collection procedures and orbital physics are built into the retro pixel-art experience.

Factors we considered

While developing the game, we had to balance scientific accuracy with making the experience enjoyable and understandable for students aged 11 to 14. We used real values wherever they mattered, while simplifying things like costs and masses to keep the game accessible.

We also made sure to follow the challenge brief and keep the language simple, with large buttons and picture icons to make navigation easier. The difficulty was adjusted using automated test players as well as feedback from actual playtesting. The retro design and intricate storylines are direct results of interviews we conducted. Finally, we focused on keeping the game completely free, removing the need for accounts and making sure multiplayer could work reliably on school networks.
